steps.prompt: One of these is a sentence. The other just leaves you hanging. Which is which?
steps.a: The giant squid with eyes as big as dinner plates.
steps.b: The giant squid has eyes as big as dinner plates.
steps.reveal: B is a sentence. A names something amazing, then never tells you anything about it: there’s no verb. Every sentence needs two parts: who or what it’s about (the subject) and what they do or are (the predicate).

cards.title: Subject + predicate
cards.body: The subject is who or what the sentence is about. The predicate starts with the verb and tells what the subject does or is. Together they make a complete thought: a sentence.

cards.title: Complete and simple
cards.text:
The tall girl in the red jacket | won the race.
Complete subject: The tall girl in the red jacket → simple subject: girl
Complete predicate: won the race → simple predicate (verb): won
cards.note: Find the verb first, then ask “who or what did it?” to find the subject.

cards.title: Compound subjects and predicates
cards.text:
Compound subject: Maya and Leo built a robot.
Compound predicate: Maya built the robot and tested it.
Both: Maya and Leo built the robot and tested it.
cards.note: Two subjects can share one verb, and one subject can do two things. It’s still one sentence.

cards.title: Hidden subjects
cards.body: Commands have an understood subject, “you”: (You) Close the door. So “Stop.” is a complete sentence, but “The big red door.” is not.

prompts: How do you find the subject of a long sentence? Explain your trick with one of your sentences.
When would a compound subject or predicate make your writing smoother?
